title: The prayer never stopped
hookLine: empires rose and fell, and the five prayers went on

lines: THE LIST OF WHAT'S STILL HERE.
cards: Make a list of what's gone. The caliphs of Damascus. The caliphs of Baghdad.
The courts of Cordoba and Cairo. Sultans, viziers, banners, coins nobody spends anymore. This path has spent a year watching them rise and fall.
Now make the other list, of what's still here. It's shorter: at dawn tomorrow, somewhere, someone will wash their face, hands and feet, stand on a mat, and say God is greatest.
Then at noon, in the afternoon, at sunset, at night. The same five prayers people prayed under those rulers. Today: the prayer never stopped.

teach.h: PRAYER AT FIXED HOURS, TIED TO THE SUN.
teach.b: Why did the prayer outlast the empires? Start with the Qur'an. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers."

Fixed hours, tied not to a palace, a capital or a king, but to the sun, which no dynasty owns. When a ruler fell, the sun still rose, and the time for dawn prayer still came. Second, the prayer was built not to stop.

teach.h: IN FEAR: STANDING OR ON HORSEBACK.
teach.b: The Qur'an says that if you are in fear, you pray standing or on horseback, however you can, and when you're safe again you remember God as He taught you. Travelers shorten it. The sick pray sitting, or lying down.
The form bends; the prayer doesn't break. Third, it was the Prophet's own last concern.

teach.h: HIS LAST WORDS: THE PRAYER, THE PRAYER.
teach.b: A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud records that among his last words, peace be upon him, was the prayer, the prayer, and care for those under your hand.

teach.h: NO CALIPH NEEDED, SO NONE COULD END IT.
teach.b: Of all the things he could have left as final words, he pointed there. Fourth, the history in that light.
The prayer didn't depend on a caliph, so it didn't fall with one. A farmer's dawn prayer in a village never needed the court's permission.
That's how a faith outlived its own empires, one person at a time, five times a day.
And it speaks to any life going through its own rise and fall, a job ending, a move, an illness: the anchor that holds is the one that doesn't depend on the weather.

how: Muslims pray five times a day at times set by the sun (dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night); travelers may shorten some prayers, and the sick may pray sitting or lying down.

games.q: what does “the prayer never stopped” mean?
o: the daily prayers outlasted every empire
Muslims must pray all day without a break
the call to prayer is broadcast nonstop

games.q: the prayer never stopped — tap the pairs.

s: the prayer times were set by the caliph's court
the Qur'an speaks of fixed hours, and the times follow the sun.
the Qur'an allows prayer standing or on horseback in times of fear
the form bends; the prayer doesn't break.
a hadith records the prayer among the Prophet's last words
Sunan Abi Dawud: the prayer, the prayer, and care for those under your hand.

games.q: you're on a road in danger. you can't stop and dismount, and the time for prayer has come. what does the Qur'an say to do?
o: pray as you can, standing or on horseback.
wait until you're safe, however long it takes, and pray it late.
games.why: Qur'an 2:239 says that in fear you pray standing or on horseback, and when you're safe again, you remember God as He taught you. the prayer bends; it doesn't stop.

practice: Look at the light through the nearest window: is the sun high, slanting, low, or gone? That light is the prayer's clock.
If you pray, decide where you'll be when the next prayer comes and how you'll step away for it; if you don't, choose that moment anyway, to stop for one breath and notice the light.

wordCard.voice: The prayer never stopped. Empires rose and fell, and the five daily prayers, tied to the sun, went on through all of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the ritual prayer, prayed five times a day.

carryVoice: Your line: the prayer went on. Empires fell, and the dawn prayer still came. I'll be here tomorrow.
